newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Southeast Asian airlines cancel Cambodia flights.
newsitem.headline: Southeast Asian airlines cancel Cambodia flights.

text.p: Malaysia Airlines (MAS) and Singapore-based SilkAir have joined other southeast Asian airlines in cancelling flights to Phnom Penh following the outbreak of fighting in the Cambodian capital.
A traffic officer for Singapore Airlines unit SilkAir, which flies to Cambodia daily, told Reuters on Saturday it was cancelling its Sunday flight but had made no decision about flights beyond that.
"At the moment it's only for tomorrow," he said, adding that he understood the Phnom Penh airport would be closed on Sunday.
SilkAir did operate its flight into and out of Phnom Penh on Saturday morning, other SilkAir employees said.

In Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia Airlines (MAS) said on Saturday: "Following recent political developments in Phnom Penh, Malaysia Airlines has, in the interest of the safety of its passengers, decided to cancel its flights to and from Phnom Penh tomorrow."
MAS has one flight on Sunday to Phnom Penh, which returns on the same day.

Earlier, airline employees in Bangkok said the major airlines flying into Phnom Penh from there had cancelled all flights to the Cambodian capital for Saturday and possibly Sunday due to the current tense political situation.

"Both of our flights today were cancelled and they will be cancelled tomorrow also," a Royal Air Cambodge ticket agent in Bangkok told Reuters. "It is because of the political problem there, and we fear for our passenger's safety."
Thai Airways also cancelled its flights on Saturday after fighting broke out just a few kilometres from the airport.
A Reuter cameraman on flight TG696 on Saturday morning said the plane had almost arrived in Phnom Penh when it was told to return to Bangkok.

At least one Vietnam Airlines flight took off from Phnom Penh in the afternoon, Cambodian airline sources said. Fighting resumed near the airport shortly afterwards and it was not clear if any other planes were able to leave.
A security official at Phnom Penh airport told Reuters airport officials had not yet decided if they would open the airport on Sunday. He said the decision would be taken in the morning.

Fighting erupted early on Saturday and continued intermittently through the day as forces loyal to powerful Second Prime Minister Hun Sen moved against troops loyal to his rival, First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh.

Authorities imposed a curfew in Phnom Penh after the day of clashes. In a statement broadcast on national television and radio, Phnom Penh municipal authorities said the curfew was being imposed from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m.
The fighting appeared to have subsided as the curfew came into effect though the city remained tense and one official reported clusters of rival troops in various parts of the city.
